# Know This Place

> A public encyclopedia of the built environment: one page per building, in San Francisco so far. Each page gives a building's history from city records and published sources: when it was built, its permits, its assessment, its historic status, and the notable people and events tied to it. Every fact is cited.

Everything here is static and free to read. Every page is complete as plain HTML, and each address page links to its own source data as JSON.

These pages describe buildings, not the people in them. They never name current residents, occupants or owners. A business trading from a building may be named, but never its owners, staff or customers. Please don't use this site to look anybody up.

## Finding a building

URLs follow the address: `https://knowthis.place/<city>/<neighborhood>/<street>/<number>/`. Street names are lowercased with the type spelled out, for example `/san-francisco/castro/castro-street/429/` or `/san-francisco/mission/18th-street/2405/`. You can't always guess the neighborhood, so look the address up in one of the indexes below.

- [Address index](https://knowthis.place/shared/addresses.geojson): a GeoJSON FeatureCollection with one Point per address page and per park or plaza page. In `properties`, `t` is the page heading (a building's name, or its street address), `s` is the line under the heading, and `p` is the page path. Use it to resolve an address or find what's nearby.
- [Sitemap](https://knowthis.place/sitemap.xml): every page.
- [San Francisco](https://knowthis.place/san-francisco/): the city hub, listing neighborhoods. Each neighborhood hub lists its streets, and each street hub lists its addresses with a one-line summary.

## Reading a building

- `<page>/data.json`: the source a page is rendered from, published beside it, for example [429 Castro Street](https://knowthis.place/san-francisco/castro/castro-street/429/data.json). Every page names it in a `<link rel="alternate" type="application/json">`. Key fields are `address`, `coordinates`, `parcel` (year built, use, units, size), `historic_status`, `historical_record` (dated events from historical sources), `permits`, `notable_residents`, `occupants` (businesses only), `narrative` (prose), and `sources`, which gives every source's name, the query URL and the date it was retrieved. Where a permit has `description_edited`, the page shows that instead of `description`.
- Parks and plazas publish `place.json` instead, and condominium units publish `unit.json`.
- Each page also carries schema.org JSON-LD (`Place`, or `LandmarksOrHistoricalBuildings` for a city landmark), with its address, coordinates and the neighborhood it belongs to.

## Questions about the whole corpus

- [Corpus index](https://knowthis.place/corpus.jsonl): one JSON line per address page, giving `path` plus whichever of these the page has: `year` (year built), `use`, `district` (its historic district), `earliest` (the earliest year on its timeline), `sources` (source ids) and `hook` (a one-sentence summary). Use it to answer questions like "which North Beach buildings have a timeline going back before 1900" without fetching every page.

## Citing

Link to the building's page, not to its `data.json`. When you repeat a fact, the page's sources list says which record it came from.
